question_text: What are the primary learning-related use-cases for AI tools described by dyslexic learners in online discussions?
How do dyslexic users describe the role of assistive technology accommodations like laptops for exams, extra time, or browser extensions in supporting their learning?
What specific reading-support features, such as coloured overlays, reading guides, bionic reading, or adjustable spacing, do dyslexic users describe as more helpful than font changes alone?
How is AI described as part of everyday study routines compared with one-off or occasional use?
How do reported AI use-cases differ between school, university, and work-related learning contexts?
In what ways do learners use AI to support idea generation, task understanding, or organisation of thoughts during study?
What benefits and failure modes do dyslexic learners report when using AI tools for different learning tasks?
When do users describe AI outputs as inaccurate, too generic, confusing, or not aligned with what they were trying to express?
In what ways do learners describe AI as helping themparticipatemore effectively in education or work-based learning environments?
In what situations do users describe AI as offering limited value compared with other assistive tools, accommodations, or personal coping strategies?
What concerns do dyslexic learners raise about over-reliance on AI, reduced skill development, or uncertainty about whether they are really learning?
How do learners describe AI improving clarity, confidence, or speed when completing learning-related work?
Under what conditions are AI tools described as helpful, supportive, or inclusive for dyslexic learners?
How do parents of dyslexic ordysgraphicchildren describe their experiences building,seeking, or customizing AI tools when existing solutions and school accommodations fall short?
What role do accessibility, ease of use, and low effort play in whether AI tools are experienced as inclusive?
How do dyslexic learners and their families describe negotiating with schools or teachers to gain acceptance of AI tools, dictation, or typing as legitimate accommodations rather than as shortcuts?
What user practices, such as prompting, checking outputs, or combining AI with other tools, are associated with more positive experiences?
How do task type, context, or severity of difficulty shape whether AI is perceived as supportive?
How are AI-based supports discussed in relation to broader educational challenges and support structures, including institutional accommodations and personal coping strategies?
In what ways is AI discussed as complementing, replacing, or compensating for existing support structures?
What gaps in school, university, or workplace support lead learners to turn to AI tools?

How do dyslexic learners describe the legitimacy and acceptance of AI-based accommodations within formal IEPs or institutional support plans compared to traditional accommodations like extra time or dictation?
How are concerns about fairness, legitimacy, or dependency discussed when AI is used alongside institutional accommodations?
How do learners position AI within their wider personal coping strategies for reading, writing, organisation, or communication?
How have discussions of AI tools among dyslexic learners changed over time in terms of prevalence, tone, and perceived role in learning support?
What do dyslexic learners say about community attitudes, rules, orskepticismtoward AI-built tools, and how does this affect their willingness to try or recommend such tools?
How have perceived benefits and risks of AI evolved as these tools have become more widely available?
How has the volume of AI-related discussion among dyslexic learners changed over time?
How have the main reported uses of AI shifted over time, for example from general curiosity to everyday academic or workplace support?
